items.body:
Mohalla no longer asks you to choose a city. Wherever you are — at home, at work, or travelling — prayer times, the Qibla bearing and distance, nearby mosques, Azan notifications and the countdown on Home are all calculated from your phone's GPS location.

If GPS is briefly unavailable, the app falls back to your last known location and says so honestly on screen. Your location never leaves your phone: there is no server, and nothing is uploaded anywhere.

You can still choose your calculation method (Karachi, ISNA, Muslim World League, Egyptian, Makkah) and your Asr madhab (Hanafi or Shafi'i) in Settings, and you can still set your own masjid's Jamaat times — those now override the calculated times for Azan as well.
items.summary: No more picking a city by hand. Prayer times, Qibla direction, nearby mosques, Azan and the countdown all come from your phone's GPS location now.
items.title: Prayer times now follow your GPS location

items.body:
Quran recitation no longer needs the internet. Open any surah and tap "Download audio for offline listening" — the surah downloads once, and after that its verses play from your phone, even in airplane mode.

Downloads are one surah at a time, on purpose: the full Quran is more than 1 GB of audio, so it is never bundled with the app and there is no "download all" button. A failed download picks up where it stopped, and you can delete a surah's audio from the same place you downloaded it to free space.

The Quran text itself was already fully offline. With downloaded audio, the whole reading and listening experience now works without a connection.
items.summary: Each surah can now be downloaded for offline listening. The recitation is the same Alafasy audio the app streams today.
items.title: Listen to the Quran offline, surah by surah

items.body:
Until now, Azan notifications only worked if you had opened Mohalla at least once since the phone started. After a restart, they stayed silent until the next launch.

That is fixed: when the phone restarts, Mohalla quietly reschedules today's Azan from your saved location and settings, without opening the app at all.

One thing still depends on the phone's settings: notifications and exact alarms must be allowed for Mohalla (Settings → Apps → Mohalla). If the app was force-stopped, Android will not run it at boot until you open it once — that is an Android rule no app can work around.
items.summary: Azan notifications are now rescheduled automatically when the phone restarts — you no longer have to open the app first.
items.title: Azan now works after a phone restart

items.body:
Prayer times are calculated, and different regions use different conventions for Fajr and Isha. In Settings → Prayer calculation you can now choose:

• Karachi — University of Islamic Sciences, Karachi. The default, and the right choice for Pakistan.
• ISNA — Islamic Society of North America, for the USA and Canada.
• Muslim World League — used in much of Europe and elsewhere.
• Egyptian — Egyptian General Authority of Survey.
• Makkah — Umm al-Qura University, for Saudi Arabia.

Asr has its own choice: Hanafi (Asr starts when the shadow is twice the object's length — the common practice in Pakistan) or Shafi'i (when the shadow equals the object's length, about an hour earlier).

If you are unsure, keep the default. And if your masjid announces its own Jamaat times, set those in Settings — your masjid's times always win over the calculation.
items.summary: Karachi, ISNA, Muslim World League, Egyptian or Makkah — and Hanafi or Shafi'i Asr. What the choices mean, and which one to pick.
items.title: Choose your prayer calculation method

items.body:
The Prophet ﷺ would fast often in Sha'ban, the month before Ramadan — not to tire himself out, but to arrive ready. You can do the same in a small way:

• Fast Mondays and Thursdays, even just one day a week, so the first fast does not come as a shock.
• Read a little Quran every day — even one page — so daily recitation is already a habit when Ramadan begins.
• Fix one habit now: an early night, a smaller dinner, or a phone-free hour after Maghrib.
• Sort out Zakat early. Work out what you owe before the month starts, so giving in Ramadan is a joy, not a rush.

Use the Prayer Tracker in Mohalla to keep the streak going. Small, steady deeds are the ones that last — that is the whole point of preparation.
items.summary: Ramadan is not a switch you flip on the first fast. A few small habits started now make the month feel completely different.
items.title: Preparing your heart for Ramadan

items.body:
Zakat is 2.5% of your wealth — cash, bank savings, gold, silver and trade goods — that you have held for one full lunar year and that is above the nisab (the minimum threshold, roughly the value of 85 grams of gold or 595 grams of silver).

It is not paid on the house you live in, the car you drive, or your personal belongings. It is paid on wealth that sits and grows.

Who receives it? The Quran (9:60) lists eight categories, starting with the poor and the needy. Your local masjid or a trusted charity can help you reach them.

Mohalla has a Zakat Calculator under More → Zakat Calculator: enter your cash, gold and silver and it works out the 2.5% for you. If you are unsure whether Zakat applies to you, ask your local imam — this guide is a starting point, not a fatwa.
items.summary: 2.5% of savings held for a full lunar year above the nisab. The essentials, in plain words — plus the calculator in this app.
items.title: What is Zakat, and who must pay it?

items.body:
The Prophet ﷺ said that Allah has ninety-nine names, and whoever learns them will enter Paradise (Bukhari & Muslim). "Learns" here means more than memorising the sounds — it means knowing what each name means and living by it.

A simple way to start: one name a day. Ar-Rahman — the Most Merciful: when you ask for mercy, you know exactly who you are asking. Al-Razzaq — the Provider: when money is tight, your worry has somewhere to go. Al-Sabur — the Most Patient: a reminder to be patient yourself.

Mohalla lists all 99 names under More → 99 Names of Allah, with Arabic, transliteration and meaning. Pick one each morning, read its meaning, and try to call on Allah by that name in your duas that day.
items.summary: One name a day, with its meaning, takes about three months to finish the list — and it changes how you make dua.
items.title: The 99 Names of Allah: a daily practice

items.body:
The Prophet ﷺ called Friday the best day on which the sun rises (Muslim). Three things make it worth preparing for:

• Surah Al-Kahf. Reading it on Friday is a well-known Sunnah — the reward described in the hadith is light between the two Fridays.
• Durood in abundance. Friday is the day the Prophet ﷺ specifically asked for more blessings to be sent upon him.
• Arriving early. The hadith about the angels recording names at the masjid door is a reminder that the early rows are worth the effort.

There is also an hour on Friday when duas are answered — the scholars differ on exactly when, but many point to the last hour before Maghrib. Keep a dua or two ready for that hour. It costs nothing to ask.
items.summary: Surah Al-Kahf, plenty of durood, and arriving early. What makes Friday special, and how to make the most of it.
items.title: Jumu'ah: the best day of the week

items.body:
Going for Hajj or Umrah is a once-in-a-lifetime journey for most of us, and the practical side deserves as much attention as the spiritual side:

• Documents first: passport validity (at least six months), visa, and vaccination certificates. Start months early — approvals take time.
• Health: see your doctor, sort out any medication, and walk daily for a few weeks before travel. The rites involve a lot of walking.
• Money: budget for the package, food, transport and gifts — and keep an emergency amount separate.
• Learn the rites before you go: the steps of Tawaf, Sa'i and the duas for each stage. Knowing them in advance means you can focus on worship instead of figuring things out on the spot.
• Travel light, and take a small dua book or use the Duas section in Mohalla.

And the simplest advice of all, from everyone who has been: be patient with the crowds. You are a guest of the Most Merciful — patience is part of the worship.
items.summary: Documents, health, money and duas — the practical list to sort out months before you travel, not days.
items.title: Hajj and Umrah: a first-timer's checklist
